4
An analogue ammeter with a range of 0–250 mA is connected into an electrical circuit. The
diagram shows the ammeter’s display.
5
0
10
What is the reading on the ammeter?
A
76 mA
B
165 mA
C
183 mA
D
190 mA

hints: Notice the dial is marked 0 to 10 but the ammeter range is 0-250 mA, so the numbers on the dial are not in mA.
Connect full scale to full range: dial reading 10 must equal $250\text{ mA}$, so find how many mA one small dial unit represents.
Read the pointer position on the 0-10 dial to about 7.6, then multiply by the mA per dial unit to get the current.
walkthrough: Identify the two scales: the printed dial runs 0 to 10 with 5 in the centre, while the electrical range is $0-250\text{ mA}$.
Use the full-scale rule: dial $10$ corresponds to $250\text{ mA}$, so $1$ dial unit $= 250/10 = 25\text{ mA}$.
Read the pointer on the dial: it points a little beyond 7.5, at about 7.6, with each small division $0.2$ dial units.
Calculate the current: $I = 7.6 \times 25\text{ mA} = 190\text{ mA}$ with a unit check in $\text{mA}$.
Match $190\text{ mA}$ to the options. This is option D.

A.explanation: 76 mA takes the scale number about 7.6 and multiplies by 10, ignoring that full scale 10 means $250\text{ mA}$.

B.explanation: 165 mA is too low and would correspond to a pointer near 6.6 on the 0-10 scale, to the left of the shown position.

C.explanation: 183 mA would correspond to about 7.3 on the 0-10 scale and under-reads the pointer which is just past the mark beyond 7.5.

D.explanation: A scale reading of about 7.6 on a 0-10 scale scaled to $250\text{ mA}$ gives $7.6 \times 25\text{ mA} = 190\text{ mA}$.
